name: Systems Development Life Cycle
description: The systems development life cycle (SDLC) describes the typical phases and progression during the development of a computer-based system, from inception to retirement. It is analogous to the life cycle of a living organism from birth to death. The SDLC does not prescribe how engineers should work — it describes the natural sequence of phases that a system passes through.

steps.name: Conceptualize — Investigate feasibility and determine whether to proceed
steps.description:
🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, during conceptualization (a.k.a. conceptual design, system investigation, feasibility), options and priorities are considered. A feasibility study determines whether the development effort is worthwhile.

Activities include: understanding user need, cost estimation, benefit analysis, and resource analysis. The study should address operational, financial, technical, human factors, and legal/political concerns.

This phase establishes the functional baseline. The central question is not what to build, but whether to build at all — and if so, which option among alternatives offers the best balance of cost, benefit, and risk.

Think deeply about what assumptions underlie the perceived need. What alternatives to building a new system exist? What would happen if we did nothing?

SequentialThinking.reason: Feasibility assessment requires disciplined evaluation of operational, financial, technical, human factors, and legal/political dimensions — the go/no-go decision is the highest-stakes judgment in the entire lifecycle

SearchMemories.reason: Find prior feasibility analyses, related system histories, and lessons learned from similar projects

stop_conditions: User need articulated and validated
Feasibility study completed covering operational, financial, technical, human factors, and legal concerns
Cost estimates and benefit analysis documented
Resource requirements identified and availability confirmed
Go/no-go decision made with documented rationale
Functional baseline established

steps.name: Requirements Analysis — Understand the problem and determine what is needed
steps.description:
🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, requirements analysis (a.k.a. preliminary design) involves understanding the problem and determining what is needed. This often involves engaging users to define requirements and recording them in a requirements specification document.

This phase establishes the allocated baseline. The central question shifts from whether to build to what to build. Distinguish between functional requirements (what the system must do) and non-functional requirements (quality attributes the system must exhibit).

Think deeply about what stakeholders say they want versus what they actually need. What requirements are implicit but unstated? What constraints exist that stakeholders haven't mentioned?

SequentialThinking.reason: Eliciting requirements demands systematic exploration of stated and unstated needs, distinguishing wants from needs, and resolving conflicting stakeholder priorities

BuildContext.reason: Map the problem domain to understand existing knowledge, related systems, and domain constraints

stop_conditions: Problem clearly understood and articulated
Users and stakeholders engaged for requirements elicitation
Functional requirements captured and documented
Non-functional requirements defined (performance, security, usability, etc.)
Requirements specification document produced
Allocated baseline established
Requirements traceable to the user needs identified during conceptualization

steps.name: Design — Plan the solution architecture and detailed design
steps.description:
🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, during the design phase (a.k.a. detail design), a solution is planned. The plan can include high-level information such as describing major system components, and low-level information such as functions, screen layout, business rules, and process flow.

The design is informed by the requirements — the design must satisfy each requirement. It may be recorded as textual documents, functional hierarchy diagrams, example screen images, business rules, process diagrams, pseudo-code, and data models.

This phase produces the product baseline. Think deeply about architectural trade-offs. What design patterns fit the requirements? What are the implications of each design choice for future maintainability and evolution?

SequentialThinking.reason: Architectural decisions involve evaluating trade-offs across multiple dimensions (performance, maintainability, cost, complexity) — systematic reasoning prevents premature commitment to suboptimal designs

SearchMemories.reason: Find proven design patterns, architectural precedents, and lessons from similar systems

stop_conditions: High-level architecture documented (major components and their relationships)
Detailed design completed (functions, screen layouts, business rules, process flows)
Data model defined
Every requirement traceable to a design element
Design reviewed and approved
Product baseline established

steps.name: Construct — Realize the system through coding and integration
steps.description:
Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, during construction (a.k.a. implementation, production), the system is realized. Based on the design, hardware and software components are created and integrated.

This phase includes testing sub-components and components and the integration of some components, but typically does not include testing at the complete system level. It may also include the development of training materials such as user manuals and help files.

This phase produces the updated product baseline. Focus on building what was designed — deviations from design should trigger a return to the design phase rather than ad hoc changes during construction.

SearchMemories.reason: Reference design documents, coding standards, and integration patterns from the knowledge graph

stop_conditions: Software and hardware components created per design specification
Sub-component and component testing completed
Component integration tested
Training materials developed (user manuals, help files)
Updated product baseline established
Code and build artifacts ready for system-level acceptance testing

steps.name: Acceptance — Test the complete system against customer expectations
steps.description:
Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, the acceptance phase (a.k.a. system testing) is about testing the complete system to ensure that it meets customer expectations (requirements). This is distinct from the component-level and integration testing performed during construction.

User acceptance testing (UAT) validates that the system as a whole satisfies the requirements specification produced during requirements analysis. Every requirement should be verified. Defects found here may require returning to construction or even design for resolution.

SearchMemories.reason: Reference requirements specification and acceptance criteria from earlier phases

stop_conditions: Complete system tested end-to-end
Every requirement in the requirements specification verified
User acceptance testing (UAT) completed with customer participation
Critical defects resolved or documented with remediation plan
Acceptance decision recorded — system meets customer expectations
System approved for deployment

steps.name: Deploy — Deliver the system to users and transition to operational use
steps.description:
Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, the deployment phase (a.k.a. implementation) involves the logistics of delivery to the customer. Some systems are deployed as a single instance (e.g. in the cloud) where deployment may be ad hoc and manual. Some systems are built in quantity and are associated with manufacturing processes and commissioning.

This phase may include training users to use the system and transitioning future development to support staff. The system moves from a development context to an operational context.

stop_conditions: System delivered to customer environment
Deployment logistics completed (installation, configuration, commissioning)
Users trained on system operation
Support staff transitioned for future development and maintenance
Monitoring and operational procedures established
System operational in production environment

steps.name: Maintain — Support operations, resolve issues, and manage evolution
steps.description:
🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, during the maintenance phase (a.k.a. operation, utilization, support), development is largely inactive although this phase does include customer support for resolving user issues and recording suggestions for improvement.

Fixes and enhancements are handled by returning to the first phase (conceptualization). For minor changes, the cycle may be significantly abbreviated compared to initial development.

Think deeply about what patterns are emerging in support requests. What systemic issues indicate design limitations? When does a maintenance fix warrant a full cycle return to conceptualization versus an abbreviated cycle?

SequentialThinking.reason: Distinguishing between minor fixes (abbreviated cycle) and systemic issues (full return to conceptualization) requires judgment about root causes, technical debt accumulation, and system evolution trajectory
focus_areas: Issue triage and root cause analysis

WriteMemory.reason: Document recurring issues, enhancement patterns, and evolution decisions as institutional knowledge for future lifecycle iterations

stop_conditions: User issues resolved or escalated with documented resolution
Suggestions for improvement recorded and prioritized
Recurring issue patterns identified and analyzed
Decision made for each issue: abbreviated fix cycle vs. full return to conceptualization
System performance and health metrics reviewed
Evolution roadmap updated based on operational experience
next_actions: Return to conceptualization for enhancements requiring a full cycle
Proceed to decommission when system reaches end-of-life

steps.name: Decommission — Retire the system and manage end-of-life transition
steps.description:
🧠 SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED: Use the SequentialThinking tool to work through this systematically.

Per the Wikipedia SDLC article, decommission (a.k.a. disposition, retirement, phase-out) is when the system is removed from use, i.e. when it reaches end-of-life.

This phase requires careful planning to ensure data preservation, user migration, and orderly shutdown. Think deeply about what dependencies exist on this system. What data must be archived? What users or downstream systems need to be migrated? What is the transition plan to replacement systems or manual processes?

Decommission is the natural terminus of every system's lifecycle. Planning for it early (even during conceptualization) leads to systems that are easier to retire gracefully.

SequentialThinking.reason: End-of-life decisions involve complex dependency analysis, data preservation requirements, migration planning, and stakeholder impact assessment — premature or poorly planned decommission can cause downstream failures

WriteMemory.reason: Document decommission decisions, lessons learned, and archival locations as institutional memory for future reference

stop_conditions: End-of-life decision documented with rationale
All system dependencies identified and addressed
Data preservation and archival completed
Users migrated to replacement systems or alternative processes
Downstream systems transitioned away from dependencies
System removed from operational use
Lessons learned documented for future system lifecycles
next_actions: Apply lessons learned to future conceptualization phases
